title: The walls of Jericho (Joshua 6)
hookLine: seven days of marching, trumpets, a shout; readers across traditions wrestle honestly with the violence of the conquest stories
tomorrow: As for me and my house

cards: "Ye shall not shout, nor make any noise with your voice, neither shall any word proceed out of your mouth." That is Joshua's order to an army. Not sharpen your swords.
Be quiet. Jericho is shut up tight. Once a day for six days, Israel walks around the city: armed men, then seven priests blowing trumpets of rams' horns, then the ark, and not one word.
On the seventh day they circle it seven times. The priests blow, the people shout with a great shout, and the text says the wall fell down flat. But the chapter doesn't stop when the wall falls.

teach.b: The verse after the shout, in the King James Bible: "And they utterly destroyed all that was in the city, both man and woman, young and old, and ox, and sheep, and ass, with the edge of the sword."
Read slowly, it's hard to hear.
The Hebrew word behind it is cherem: something devoted to God and taken out of ordinary use, which in war meant destruction. The King James renders it accursed.
Jews and Christians have both lived with this chapter, in different ways.

Some read it as history: a brutal practice of the ancient world, told plainly, not a pattern for today. Some Christian teachers have read the battles as a picture of an inner war against greed, pride and fear.
Some read the conquest beside the parts of the Bible that push against it, and the text itself pushes. In this very chapter, the one household spared is Canaanite: Rahab's, under the red line.
And just before the march, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword and asks, "Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?"

teach.h: NAY: CAPTAIN OF THE LORD'S HOST.
teach.b: The answer: "Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come." Joshua falls on his face. God is not simply drafted onto Israel's side; Joshua is the one asked to bow.
None of these readings makes it easy.
Wrestling with a hard text out loud is one honest way to read scripture, and Genesis has a picture of it: Jacob wrestles through the night until daybreak, and comes away blessed, and limping.

how: Christians read Joshua 6 in different ways, as ancient history, as a picture of spiritual struggle, or beside texts that push against it, and some Bible study groups take time to discuss its violence openly.

games.q: you're Joshua, near Jericho. a man with a drawn sword stands in front of you. you ask: are you for us, or for our enemies? what does he answer?
o: neither: he comes as captain of the Lord's host.
games.why: "Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come." Joshua falls on his face. the question turns around.

practice: If you can, walk once around your block or your room without a word; if you can't, sit and let your attention move slowly along the edges of the space.
Bring to mind one hard passage and don't solve, defend or dismiss it: just walk around it quietly, the way Israel walked around a wall. If you pray, bring it to God just as it is.

wordCard.voice: Cherem. Hebrew for devoted, set apart for God and taken out of ordinary use: the word behind Jericho's destruction.

orig.note: Hebrew: devoted, set apart for God and taken out of ordinary use. the KJV renders it accursed in Joshua 6:17.

carryVoice: Your line: wrestle with hard texts. Not skip them, not settle them too fast. That's day seven hundred.
